conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor on call. I understand you’re here for abdominal pain. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been about a week. My whole belly feels crampy and swollen, like I’m distended. It’s getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes—nausea and loose stools, several times a day. I threw up once since I got to the ER, just clear stuff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any blood in the stool? Any fevers or chills at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood. No fevers that I noticed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you have a gastrostomy tube. Any issues with it recently—leakage, pain at the site, or trouble with feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Five days ago it was leaking, and they changed the tube. The site looks okay now, but the pain kept getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have you been getting large residuals when you check the tube, or trouble flushing it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No big residuals. It flushes fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: What have you taken for pain at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just Tylenol. I can’t take NSAIDs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right—no NSAIDs or aspirin because of ulcer risk after bypass. We’re going to check labs and get imaging to make sure there’s no obstruction or internal hernia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared it’s another blockage. It feels like everything is stuck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. With your Roux-en-Y history, we take that seriously. We’ll start with an abdominal X-ray now, and likely a CT scan after that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: While we’re waiting, we’ll keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—and give IV fluids and nausea medicine. Is your pain constant or comes in waves?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Waves. Cramping. Then it eases a little and comes back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray is back. It shows a non-obstructive bowel gas pattern—no free air and no clear signs of a blockage on that test.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: An X-ray can miss things, especially after bypass surgery. Given your symptoms, we still want the CT scan to look for obstruction or an internal hernia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I going to need surgery tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t know yet. If the CT shows a surgical problem, we’d talk about next steps right away. If it’s reassuring, we may observe you, treat symptoms, and restart tube feeds carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your bloodwork so far looks reassuring—white blood cell count is normal and your lactate is normal, which makes a dangerous lack of blood flow to the bowel less likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I still feel bloated though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue IV fluids overnight and keep monitoring. If you have more vomiting, worsening pain, or you feel feverish, tell the nurse right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night? Any more vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more vomiting. Still nauseated on and off. The cramps are a little better with the meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’re going to proceed with the CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast this morning to evaluate for obstruction or internal hernia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the contrast safe with my tube and bypass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll get IV contrast, and you’ll also drink oral contrast if you can tolerate it. It helps us see the bowel pathways after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: CT results are back. The good news: no signs of bowel obstruction, and no CT signs of an internal hernia. Your gastrostomy tube position looks unchanged in the gastric remnant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing is wrong? But I’m still hurting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT rules out the big emergencies we worry about. Pain can still happen from cramping and irritation even without a blockage. Right now, since you’re stable and the imaging is reassuring, the plan is observation and symptom control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the tube site—could it be infected from when it leaked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: On exam the tube site looks normal—no redness, swelling, or drainage—and you haven’t had fevers. We’ll keep watching closely, but there’s no sign of infection at this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Since your nausea is improving and the CT is reassuring, we’ll start by giving you water and then re-trial your tube feeds slowly. If symptoms worsen, we’ll pause and reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous to restart feeds. What if it makes the cramping worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a reasonable concern. We’ll start gently and monitor for pain, bloating, vomiting, and residuals. You can tell us right away if it feels like too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did the water and the initial tube feed trial go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So far okay. Some mild cramps, but not like before. No vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll continue the feeds as tolerated and keep your nausea medication available as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have something stronger for pain? Tylenol isn’t enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll use a multimodal plan and transition you to oral pain medication as you tolerate intake. We can use liquid oxycodone as needed, and we’ll continue your gabapentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that make me too sleepy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can. We’ll use the lowest effective dose, and we’ll watch for drowsiness. No driving or operating machinery while taking it after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning check-in. Any fevers, chest pain, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. Just tired. The pain is much better today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your vitals have been stable, and there’s been no sign of infection or bleeding. Are you tolerating tube feeds and water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. No big residuals. Nausea is mostly controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll keep encouraging you to get up and walk, use the incentive spirometer, and we’ll continue blood clot prevention with the boots and heparin while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I eat real food again? I’m on that Stage III diet, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—Stage III diet only for now. Don’t advance it on your own until your follow-up. Also avoid straws and chewing gum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal exam remains soft with only mild tenderness, and the tube site still looks fine. If things stay stable overnight, we’ll plan for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home? I don’t want to end up back here again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back or call your surgeon if you get fever over 101.5, severe abdominal pain, pain not relieved by your meds, severe nausea or vomiting, severe bloating, chest pain, shortness of breath, or if you can’t keep down fluids or tolerate tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve been stable and tolerating water and tube feeds. Pain controlled?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I still get some cramps, but it’s manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll discharge you home today. You’ll continue your home meds, and remember: crush all pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Which meds am I leaving with for the stomach and pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For your GI protection and ulcer care: lansoprazole and sucralfate. For nausea: ondansetron as needed. For pain: liquid oxycodone as needed, plus your gabapentin. And continue your tube feeding formula as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take ibuprofen if the pain flares?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No—avoid all NSAIDs and aspirin. They can cause bleeding and ulcers, especially after gastric bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about activity? I’m worried I’ll pull something around the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No heavy lifting for 6 weeks. You can do moderate exercise as you feel able, but avoid abdominal exercises. Keep walking—gentle movement helps your bowels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I shower with the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you may shower. No tub baths or swimming. Call if you notice increased pain, swelling, or redness at the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go—any last questions about the CT results or the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just to confirm: the CT showed no obstruction and the tube is in the right place?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no obstruction, no internal hernia seen, and the gastrostomy tube position is unchanged in the gastric remnant. If symptoms worsen at home, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Thank you for explaining everything. I’m ready to go home.
